entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8149"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <div sID="gen12716" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1-Eccl.10.20">Ec 10:1-20</reference>.<div eID="gen12716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12717" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8149"/>1. Following up <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">Ec 9:18</reference>.<div eID="gen12717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him that is in reputation--</hi>for example, David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.14">2Sa 12:14</reference>); Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.1-1Kgs.11.43">1Ki 11:1-43</reference>); Jehoshaphat (2Ch 18:1-34; 19:2); Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.22">2Ch 35:22</reference>). The more delicate the perfume, the more easily spoiled is the ointment. Common oil is not so liable to injury. So the higher a man's religious character is, the more hurt is caused by a sinful folly in him. Bad savor is endurable in oil, but not in what professes to be, and is compounded by the perfumer ("apothecary") for, fragrance. "Flies" answer to "a little folly" (sin), appropriately, being small (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6">1Co 5:6</reference>); also, "Beelzebub" means prince of flies. "Ointment" answers to "reputation" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ec 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Ge 34:30</reference>). The verbs are singular, the noun plural, implying that each of the flies causes the stinking savor. <div eID="gen12718" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8156"/><div sID="gen12727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8156"/>8. The fatal results to kings of such an unwise policy; the wrong done to others recoils on themselves (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ec 8:9</reference>); they fall into the pit which they dug for others (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.10">Es 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15">Psa 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.27">Pr 26:27</reference>). Breaking through the wise fences of their throne, they suffer unexpectedly themselves; as when one is stung by a serpent lurking in the stones of his neighbor's garden wall (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.12">Psa 80:12</reference>), which he maliciously pulls down (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.19">Am 5:19</reference>). <div eID="gen12727" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8158"/><div sID="gen12730" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8158"/><hi type="bold">10. iron ... blunt--</hi>in "cleaving wood" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.9">Ec 10:9</reference>), answering to the "fool set in dignity" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">Ec 10:6</reference>), who wants sharpness. More force has then to be used in both cases; but "force" without judgment "endangers" one's self. Translate, "If one hath blunted his iron" [Maurer]. The preference of rash to judicious counsellors, which entailed the pushing of matters by force, proved to be the "hurt" of Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.33">1Ki 12:1-33</reference>).<div eID="gen12730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wisdom is profitable to direct--</hi>to a prosperous issue. Instead of forcing matters by main "strength" to one's own hurt (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">Ec 9:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen12731" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8159"/><div sID="gen12732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8159"/>11. A "serpent will bite" if "enchantment" is not used; "and a babbling calumniator is no better." Therefore, as one may escape a serpent by charms (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.4">Psa 58:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.5">5</reference>), so one may escape the sting of a calumniator by discretion (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.12">Ec 10:12</reference>), [Holden]. Thus, "without enchantment" answers to "not whet the edge" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.10">Ec 10:10</reference>), both expressing, figuratively, want of judgment. Maurer translates, "There is no gain to the enchanter" (Margin, "master of the tongue") from his enchantments, because the serpent bites before he can use them; hence the need of continual caution. <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.8-Eccl.10.10">Ec 10:8-10</reference>, caution in acting; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.11">Ec 10:11</reference> and following verses, caution in speaking. <div eID="gen12732" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8163"/><div sID="gen12738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8163"/><hi type="bold">15. labour ... wearieth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Is 55:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Ha 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen12738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth not how to go to the city--</hi>proverb for ignorance of the most ordinary matters (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.3">Ec 10:3</reference>); spiritually, the heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Psa 107:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.13">Mt 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.14">14</reference>). Maurer connects <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">Ec 10:15</reference> with the following verses. The labor (vexation) caused by the foolish (injurious princes, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4-Eccl.10.7">Ec 10:4-7</reference>) harasses him who "knows not how to go to the city," to ingratiate himself with them there. English Version is simpler. <div eID="gen12739" type="x-p"/>

entries.reader_content_plain: 17. son of nobles-- not merely in blood, but in virtue, the true nobility ( So 7:1 ; Is 32:5 , 8 ). in due season-- ( Ec 3:1 ), not until duty has first been attended to. for strength-- to refresh the body, not for revelry (included in "drunkenness").

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8167"/><div sID="gen12748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8167"/>19. Referring to <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.18">Ec 10:18</reference>. Instead of repairing the breaches in the commonwealth (equivalent to "building"), the princes "make a feast for laughter (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Ec 10:16</reference>), and wine maketh their life glad (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">Psa 104:15</reference>), and (but) money supplieth (answereth their wishes by supplying) all things," that is, they take bribes to support their extravagance; and hence arise the wrongs that are perpetrated (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.5">Ec 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.23">Is 1:23</reference>; 5:23). Maurer takes "all things" of the wrongs to which princes are instigated by "money"; for example, the heavy taxes, which were the occasion of Rehoboam losing ten tribes (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.4">1Ki 12:4</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen12748" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 19. Referring to Ec 10:18 . Instead of repairing the breaches in the commonwealth (equivalent to "building"), the princes "make a feast for laughter ( Ec 10:16 ), and wine maketh their life glad ( Psa 104:15 ), and (but) money supplieth (answereth their wishes by supplying) all things," that is, they take bribes to support their extravagance; and hence arise the wrongs that are perpetrated ( Ec 10:5 , 6 ; 3:16 ; Is 1:23 ; 5:23). Maurer takes "all things" of the wrongs to which princes are instigated by "money"; for example, the heavy taxes, which were the occasion of Rehoboam losing ten tribes ( 1Ki 12:4 , &c.).

The language, as applied to earthly princes knowing the "thought," is figurative. But it literally holds good of the King of kings (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.1-Ps.139.24">Psa 139:1-24</reference>), whose consciousness of every evil thought we should ever realize.<div eID="gen12750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bed-chamber--</hi>the most secret place (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.12">2Ki 6:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bird of the air, &c.--</hi>proverbial (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">Ha 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.40">Lu 19:40</reference>); in a way as marvellous and rapid, as if birds or some winged messenger carried to the king information of the curse so uttered. In the East superhuman sagacity was attributed to birds (see on <reference osisRef="Job.28.21">Job 28:21</reference>; hence the proverb). <chapter eID="Eccl.10"/>
